title: Blame without blaming the person who reformatted the file
summary: Every line points at a style cleanup instead of the change you care about. Learn the flags that see through reformatting and code movement, then make the fix permanent with a blame-ignore file.
mental_model: Blame reports the last commit that touched each line. A repo-wide cleanup touches every line, so it becomes the answer to every question. `-w`, `-C` and ignore-revs each tell blame a different category of commit to look straight through.

commit.message: Correct the dosing rate after calibration
Reformat and rename locals to house style

steps.title: Blame the file and get a useless answer
steps.why: Every line says 'Reformat and rename locals to house style'. The commit that actually changed the dosing rate from 1.0 to 1.35 is invisible, because a later cosmetic commit rewrote the same lines.
steps.expect: One commit hash on every line — the cleanup.

steps.title: Ignore whitespace-only differences
steps.why: `-w` tells blame that a line differing only in whitespace was not really changed. The `def` lines snap back to their real authors. Line 2 does not, because renaming `rate` to `dose_rate` is a genuine content change — whitespace flags cannot help there.
steps.expect: Better at the top and bottom, still wrong on the two lines that were renamed.

steps.title: Name the cosmetic commit and skip it entirely
steps.why: `--ignore-rev` makes blame look straight through one specific commit, as if it had never happened, and attribute each line to whatever touched it before. You are not guessing — you are telling git which commit was noise.
steps.expect: Lines 2 and 3 now attribute to 'Correct the dosing rate after calibration' — the answer you wanted.

verify.cmd: sh -c "git blame --ignore-rev $(git rev-parse HEAD) --line-porcelain -L 2,2 dosing.py | grep '^summary'"
verify.label: ignoring the cleanup reveals the real change

steps.title: Make it permanent, for everyone
steps.why: A `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file lists cosmetic commits by full sha. Point `blame.ignoreRevsFile` at it and every blame in the repo skips them automatically — GitHub reads the same file, so the web UI agrees.
steps.expect: Plain `git blame`, no flags, now gives the useful answer.

verify.label: plain blame is now correct for everyone
verify.hint: write the cleanup sha into .git-blame-ignore-revs and set blame.ignoreRevsFile

steps.title: Blame one range instead of a whole file
steps.why: `-L` limits blame to a line range, and takes a function name too: `-L :dose:dosing.py`. On a thousand-line file this is the difference between an answer and a wall of text.

steps.title: Track code that moved between files
steps.why: `-C` detects lines copied or moved from another file; repeating it makes git search harder. Without it, moving a function to a new file makes every line look brand new and blames the person who did the move.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Move dosing into chemistry module"

steps.expect: Lines still attribute to the calibration commit rather than to the move.

steps.title: Commit the ignore file so the team gets it
steps.why: The file is shared through the repo; the config line is per-clone. Document both, or the next person will rediscover this the hard way.
commands: git commit -m "Ignore the reformat commit in blame"

verify.label: the blame-ignore file is committed for the whole team
blame is configured to use it
blame sees through the cleanup AND the file move
verify.hint: -C follows code across files; the ignore file handles the cleanup

pitfalls: Blame answers 'which commit last touched this line', not 'who is responsible'. A rename, a reformat or a merge can all take the credit.
The ignore-revs file must contain full 40-character shas. Short ones are rejected outright.
`blame.ignoreRevsFile` is repo config, so it does not travel with a clone. Put the setup line in your contributing guide.
For 'when did this line get deleted', blame cannot help — the line is not there any more. Use `git log -S` instead.
